comparator.name: Biomedische wetenschappen
comparator.academicYear: Current curriculum for the 2026–27 cohort; checked 2026-09-27
comparator.sourceNotes: Official prospective and current-student curriculum pages establish a 180-EC degree with a 135-EC major and 45-EC profiling space. The major comprises 75 EC of required study and 60 EC of major-bound choice: seven 7.5-EC first-year compulsory courses, one 7.5-EC first-year biomedical elective, 15 EC Onderzoeksmethoden, 7.5 EC Bio-informatica, five 7.5-EC advanced major-bound electives including Moleculaire Biologie van de Cel, and the compulsory 15-EC Researchproject. The 2026–27 concept curriculum confirms exceptional component sizes. No formal named graduation route is required, so no route is imposed. The prospective site separately announces a redesigned curriculum only from September 2027.

components.name: Biomedical first-year elective
components.note: One biomedical elective is chosen from the published first-year green list; the choice remains neutral rather than inventing a specialisation.

components.name: Five advanced major-bound electives
components.note: Five of ten published major-bound electives are required, including Moleculaire Biologie van de Cel; this variable space remains open.

components.name: Researchproject
components.note: Compulsory third-year literature study plus experimental research or mini-internship and thesis.

components.name: Profileringsruimte
components.note: Open profiling space; no optional minor or other named route is imposed.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The closest match covers the programme's full biomedical core. Two direct interest clusters support coherent and substantially distinct alternatives: molecular/genetic biomedical data, and physiology/infection/translational health. Each schedule contains 24 feasible current UCR courses, the alternatives differ by at least four courses, and production stops at the maximum of three defensible alternatives.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both establish cellular and molecular foundations for human biomedical study.
Both develop molecular cell biology and biochemical mechanisms.
Both connect molecular processes and genetic information, with the explicit genome focus reinforced by Molecular Pathology & Genetics.
Both connect molecular and genetic change to disease, including cancer-relevant mechanisms.
Both integrate human physiology at organism and organ-system level.
Functional anatomy complements the comparator's tissues and organism structure.
Both connect biomedical knowledge to prevention and wider health impact.
UCR laboratory work supplies hands-on experimental practice within the comparator's broader compulsory methods component.
The advanced seminar provides research design, analysis and scholarly synthesis, but not the comparator's compulsory 15-EC thesis project.
Both develop quantitative data literacy; the comparator specifically applies it to biological information.
The first-year biomedical elective remains neutral.
The five advanced major-bound electives remain variable rather than being forced into one fictitious route.
The 45-EC profiling space remains open and is not treated as fixed comparator content.

comparator.note: Compulsory third-year literature study plus experimental research or mini-internship and thesis.
One biomedical elective is chosen from the published first-year green list; the choice remains neutral rather than inventing a specialisation.
Five of ten published major-bound electives are required, including Moleculaire Biologie van de Cel; this variable space remains open.
Open profiling space; no optional minor or other named route is imposed.

notes.text: Utrecht Biomedical Sciences has a prescribed 135-EC major, a compulsory 15-EC Researchproject and a large published biomedical elective catalogue. UCR can build strong biomedical pathways from molecular, physiological, disease, public-health and quantitative courses, but it does not reproduce Utrecht's dedicated Researchproject or every specialist elective; shared rows indicate substantive overlap rather than full equivalence.
